description: College students wanted to explore and learn about space and build related software systems and tools
summary:
ASTRA HEALTH is a health companion for astronauts on long missions to Mars, where help from Earth can be up to 44 minutes away for a round trip.

It runs on board, fully offline. Each day the astronaut does a two-minute check-in. ASTRA compares each reading with that person’s own normal range, and fixed medical rules decide how serious a change is. Machine learning spots unusual patterns and slow trends early. The app then tells the astronaut, in plain words, how they are, what to do now and when to get help. An AI assistant explains in everyday language, citing NASA and CSA sources.

Three more tools help the crew look after themselves:

a camera exercise coach that counts reps and corrects posture against bone and muscle loss;
a smartwatch connection for live heart rate;
a Medication Guide that gives the right medicine from the onboard kit, with the exact dose, after safety checks. The crew medical officer confirms it.

Everything syncs to a flight surgeon on Earth over a simulated deep-space link that has real light-time delay.

This matters because on Mars no doctor can respond in time, so the crew must be able to notice, understand and treat health problems themselves, safely.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

ASTRA HEALTH is a health system for astronauts on long missions to Mars. It runs as two copies of the same backend: a Habitat node on the spacecraft and a Ground node on Earth. They are joined by a simulated deep-space link that uses the real Earth–Mars light-time delay (from NASA JPL Horizons), and it can go down during blackouts.

The astronaut’s day:

  • Daily check-in (about 2 minutes). Vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen, blood sugar, body mass), sleep, mood, stress and symptoms. A Bluetooth smartwatch can fill in heart rate.
  • Personal normal. Each reading is compared with that astronaut’s own normal range from the last 28 days, not a textbook average.
  • Who decides what.
    • 19 versioned medical rules decide how serious a change is.
    • Machine learning (Isolation Forest plus a Mann–Kendall trend test) spots unusual days and slow drifts. It can only support a rule’s finding, never raise an urgent alert on its own.
    • An AI assistant (Claude or Gemini online, an offline template otherwise) explains the results in everyday words, citing NASA and CSA sources. It never diagnoses or chooses a medicine. Emergency words skip the AI and open the emergency procedure straight away.
  • Medication Guide. The astronaut picks the problem (headache, back pain, fever, motion sickness and more) and answers safety questions. The guide gives the medicine from the onboard kit with the exact dose, when to take it and which drawer it’s in. It first checks allergies, health conditions, other medicines, time since the last dose, 24-hour limits, stock and expiry. The crew medical officer confirms, and the flight surgeon reviews later.
  • Camera exercise coach. It counts reps and sets, corrects posture out loud and adjusts the plan to the astronaut’s condition. The video never leaves the device.
  • Flight surgeon dashboard (on Earth). Crew overview, alerts, trends, reports, photos and medicine reviews, plus instructions sent back over the delayed link.

Every record syncs between the nodes exactly once. Each batch is signed with HMAC (a shared secret key), and records are merged with clear rules, so nothing is duplicated or lost.

Benefits

  • Works without Earth or the internet. Everything runs on board, including the emergency procedures and the AI’s offline answers.
  • Personal and early. Changes are judged against each person’s own normal, and trends are caught before they become emergencies.
  • Easy to understand under stress. One sentence first (OK, Take care, or Get help now), one thing to do, details folded away. There are light and dark themes and points for good habits.
  • Safe by design. Rules decide, ML supports, the AI only explains. Doses come from a versioned medicine list, never from AI.
  • Doctors stay informed despite delays of up to 22 minutes each way.

Intended impact

On Mars, no doctor can respond in time. ASTRA helps crews notice, understand and treat health problems themselves, safely, which is the core of what NASA calls Earth-independent medical operations. On Earth, the same approach can help remote and underserved communities: Antarctic stations, ships, rural clinics, disaster zones and people managing their health at home.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL, JSON/YAML (the rules and protocols).

Backend:

  • FastAPI, SQLModel and SQLite
  • scikit-learn for machine learning
  • BM25 search over a knowledge base of cited notes
  • Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini APIs
  • WebSockets for live updates

Frontend:

  • React 19, Vite and Tailwind CSS
  • TanStack Query and Dexie for offline storage
  • an installable app (PWA)
  • three.js for the 3D body model
  • MediaPipe Pose for on-device body tracking
  • Web Bluetooth for the watch, Web Speech for voice

Data:

  • NASA DONKI (solar events), NOAA SWPC (proton flux), NASA JPL Horizons (light time)
  • the NASA Human Research Program and CSA radiation pages provided by the organizers

Hardware: a laptop and its webcam, a phone, and a standard Bluetooth heart-rate smartwatch.

Quality and deployment:

  • 312 backend tests (pytest), 52 browser tests (Playwright) and accessibility scans (axe, WCAG 2.1 AA)
  • ruff and mypy for code quality
  • Docker, Caddy, Google Cloud and Vercel for deployment

What makes it creative

  • Two real nodes with real light-time delay. Data takes real minutes to reach Earth and links can drop, as on a real mission.
  • A strict order of authority between rules, ML and AI, so the AI can never override a medical decision.
  • A camera coach with no data leaving the device: only counts and form scores are saved.
  • A Medication Guide that is safe without Earth. It combines yes/no safety questions, fixed checks, crew-officer confirmation and a review on Earth later.
  • Plain-language screens with gamification, designed for a tired, stressed astronaut rather than a doctor.

Factors our team considered

  • Safety: rules and doses that are deterministic, versioned and tested; red flags that bypass the AI; clear “not a medical device” and “demo dose” labels.
  • Communication delay and blackouts: offline first, a send queue that survives restarts, exactly-once sync.
  • Privacy: role-based access, an audit log, camera video never stored.
  • Human factors: low reading effort, accessibility, light and dark themes, voice guidance.
  • Honest data: real NASA and NOAA space-weather data; crew health data clearly marked as simulated.
  • NASA’s spaceflight health risks: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, low gravity and the closed habitat, mapped to features and sources.
